About 140 small BLUE dots (bulk water) drift by a Brownian updater the whole film: each dot takes a small random step every frame and bounces off the walls. COLOR MAP: BLUE bulk water, TEAL the stiffer layer of water lining an oily surface (and those dots, which jitter a little less widely than bulk dots while they sit in the layer), YELLOW oily (nonpolar) groups drawn as round blobs, GREEN polar beads and the bonds-and-packing term, RED the chain's lost freedom (a cost), GOLD totals and the take-home. On the right edge a vertical gauge 'water's freedom' (BLUE fill, label 30, tag 'schematic' 28 under it) rises and falls with how many dots are free. No molecular structures anywhere: beads, blobs, dots, bars. Labels size 30 or larger, full opacity, at most 5 words, at most 6 labelled things on screen. NO fade from black: the water is already drifting. In the middle, a floppy chain of 14 beads (8 GREEN polar beads, 6 YELLOW oily blobs, joined by a thin white line) wriggles through random shapes (its bead positions follow a slow noise updater). On 'folds itself' the chain curls into one compact ball, YELLOW blobs inside, GREEN beads on the outside, over 2 s. On 'second law' a chip 'second law: disorder wins?' (RED, 32) drops in above the ball and a RED '?' (48) pulses beside it. On 'Watch the water' the ball unfolds back into the wriggling chain, so the question stays open, and the camera eases in 15% toward it; the BLUE dots keep drifting and the 'water's freedom' gauge fades in at the right edge.

scenes.visual: Do not cut away: the glass of water and the wriggling chain stay at 25% opacity, dots still drifting. Over them: BIOCHEMISTRYPEDIA (TEAL), the title 'Count the Water' (TITLE_FONT 54) and a GOLD rule. Title out in the last 0.4 s; the world returns to full opacity.

scenes.tts: The second law counts total entropy. That means the protein, the water around it, and the heat they trade with their surroundings. So here is the rule. Count the water, not just the molecule.

scenes.tts: Start with one oily group, a methyl on an alanine side chain. Water cannot hydrogen bond to it. So the water touching it points its bonds along the surface. That layer has fewer ways to arrange itself: lower entropy.

scenes.tts: Pictures often draw this layer as an ice cage. That overstates it. The layer is only slightly stiffer than bulk water. But a protein has many oily groups. Around all of them, it adds up.

scenes.tts: It goes up. One cluster has less surface than six scattered groups. So less water must line it. The freed water rejoins the bulk. The groups gather mainly because the water gains freedom, not because they attract.

scenes.tts: That release is the hydrophobic effect. Near room temperature, its gain is almost all entropy. At higher temperatures, enthalpy takes a bigger share. It does at large, flat surfaces too.

scenes.tts: Fold a small protein—about a hundred residues—using round numbers near room temperature. The chain's lost freedom costs about plus five hundred fifty kilojoules per mole. Freed water gives back minus five hundred. Bonds and packing inside the fold add about minus ninety.

scenes.tts: The total is about minus forty. Folding is favored, by a small difference between big numbers. Shift the burial term by ten percent. The total moves by more than its own size. That is why one bad mutation can unfold a protein.

scenes.tts: And the second law? The water's entropy gain covers most of the chain's loss, but not quite all. The bonds inside release heat. That heat raises the entropy of the surroundings. Count everything, and total entropy rises.
